scenes.title: Ramsey's four funds
lines: Ramsey Solutions recommends spreading your investments across four kinds of mutual funds: growth and income, growth, international, and aggressive growth.
Say that after years of saving, you retire with a million dollars, a quarter of it in each, here in four American Funds that fit those labels.

scenes.title: The book's way: 8% of what's left
lines: Here's the plan as the book lays it out: take eight percent of whatever is there each January. The money can't run out, but the paycheck rises and falls with the market.
Say you retired in January 2000. The first check was eighty thousand. By 2003 it was forty-six thousand, and after 2008 it never again topped forty-five.
In its leanest year it paid thirty thousand dollars.

scenes.title: Checking Ramsey's numbers
lines: That quote rests on three numbers. Here's each one for every retirement in the four funds since 1981.

First, a twelve percent return. Across all forty-five years, the four funds did average a little over twelve. But the typical thirty-year retirement got about eleven, and only three of the sixteen reached twelve.
Second, inflation of four percent. That one held up: inflation ran lower, about three percent since 1981, and no finished retirement saw four.

Third, a nest egg growing four percent a year. Taking eight percent of what's left, the typical one grew about two percent, and none grew four. With inflation that low, it barely kept pace, and retirees from 1997 to 2008 fell behind.

scenes.title: Every retiree's range of checks
lines: Here's every retirement's range of checks so far, taking eight percent of what's left: the biggest year at the top, the leanest at the bottom, and the median year marked in between.
Among the sixteen finished retirements, the typical leanest year paid about fifty-eight thousand dollars. The worst, retiring in 1996, got by one year on forty-nine thousand.
Those who retired around 2000 have already had years between thirty and thirty-seven thousand, and their median year paid only forty to fifty.

scenes.title: Another way: never take a pay cut
lines: Ramsey suggests a cost-of-living raise every year is possible. So try it the other way: take eighty thousand the first year, then raise it with inflation and never take a cut. Back to the 2000 retiree.
The dot-com crash came first. Then in 2008 all four funds lost between thirty-five and thirty-nine percent.
The money ran out in 2013, thirteen years in. An S&P 500 index fund on its own would have run out four years sooner.

scenes.title: Every retirement since 1981
lines: Here's every retirement that started from 1981 on, each taking eighty thousand of today's dollars a year.
All sixteen that have had a full thirty years made it, and thirteen of them ended with more than the million they started with.
But ten of the twelve that started from 1997 to 2008 have already run out, most within twenty years.

scenes.title: Retiring around the book: 2002 to 2005
lines: Look closer at the four retirements around the book's release, from 2002 to 2005.
Retiring in 2003, the first year gained thirty-one percent, and by 2007 the million had grown to almost one point four. Even after 2008, it still has seven hundred thousand left.
Retiring one year earlier, in 2002, the first year lost seventeen percent. The money never got back to a million, and it ran out in 2019.
The 2004 and 2005 retirees went into 2008 with much smaller cushions, and both ran out in 2023.

scenes.title: Where things stood in 2003
lines: Now go back to when the book was written. Say its numbers stop at the start of 2003: twenty-two retirements had begun since 1981, each taking eighty thousand a year, and not one had run out.
Fifteen still had more than the million they started with, three of them more than two million.
But the five that started from 1998 to 2002 were already down to between about five hundred fifty and eight hundred thousand. All five later ran out.

scenes.title: Thirty years or twenty?
lines: So far, every retirement has had to last thirty years. What if it only had to last twenty, close to the average life expectancy at sixty-five?
At thirty years, all sixteen finished retirements lasted. But ten others ran out before reaching thirty, and nineteen are too recent to tell.
At twenty years, twenty-six have finished, and only nineteen of them lasted. Nearly the same retirements run out either way; twenty years just finishes more of them.

Taking eight percent of what's left, the money never runs out, but the worst leanest year falls from forty-nine thousand to thirty-four. And at forty thousand a year, every finished retirement lasted at both lengths.

scenes.title: What the four funds show
lines: Taking eight percent of what's left, as the book lays out, the money never ran out, but many years paid far less than the eighty thousand planned.
Taking eighty thousand with a raise every year lasted for every retirement that has had thirty years, and ran out for many that started near the 2000 peak.
At eight percent, the order of the years decides, over thirty years or twenty.
